desc:
A message is encoded with the rule 1 -> A, 2 -> B, ..., 26 -> Z. The encoded text is given as an array symbols. Each entry is either a digit 0..9, or -1, a wildcard that stands for any one digit from 1 to 9 (a wildcard is never 0).

A decoding chooses a digit for every wildcard and then cuts the digits into pieces of one or two digits, where every piece is a number from 1 to 26 without a leading zero (so 6, 12, 26 are valid; 0, 06, 27 are not). Count the decodings, where two decodings are different if they choose different digits for some wildcard or cut at different places. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

symbols = [-1]      -> 9    (the digit can be 1..9, each decodes as one letter)
symbols = [1,-1]    -> 18   (digits 11..19: 9 two-digit readings plus 9 one-by-one readings)
symbols = [-1,-1]   -> 96
symbols = [0]       -> 0
constraints: symbols[i] is -1 or a digit from 0 to 9
hints: Without wildcards this is the classic Decode Ways with a prefix DP: the last piece is one digit or two digits. Keep that skeleton.
Let dp[i] be the number of decodings of the first i symbols. Then dp[i] = dp[i-1] * one(s[i-1]) + dp[i-2] * two(s[i-2], s[i-1]), where one and two count how many digit choices make the piece valid.

one(x): 9 for a wildcard, 0 for the digit 0, otherwise 1. two(a, b): for two wildcards 15 (11..19 and 21..26); for wildcard then digit b, 2 choices (a = 1 or 2) when b ≤ 6, else 1; for digit then wildcard, 9 if a = 1, 6 if a = 2, else 0; for two digits, 1 if the number is 10..26, else 0.
editorial: The skeleton is the standard prefix DP: the last piece of the first i symbols is either the single symbol s[i-1] or the pair s[i-2], s[i-1], so dp[i] = dp[i-1] * one + dp[i-2] * two. The new part is that a piece can stand for several digit strings, and each valid substitution multiplies the number of decodings. Because the pieces of a cutting use disjoint wildcards, the counts multiply.

one(x) is 9 for a wildcard (1..9), 0 for the digit 0, and 1 for a digit 1..9. two(a, b) counts the two-digit values 10..26: both wildcards give 11..19 and 21..26, which is 15 (10 and 20 are excluded because a wildcard is never 0). Wildcard first then a digit b: the first digit may be 1 (always valid) or 2 (valid when b ≤ 6), so 2 or 1. Digit a then wildcard: 9 for a = 1 (11..19), 6 for a = 2 (21..26), otherwise 0. Two plain digits give 1 for 10..26 and 0 otherwise (this also rejects a leading 0). Using only the last two values makes it O(n) time and O(1) space, always reducing modulo 1,000,000,007.
